add_nodes.title: An engine built around an AI-designed alloy flies
add_nodes.description: A new rocket engine or major engine version flies with hot-section parts (preburner, turbine, chamber or nozzle) made from an alloy proposed by an AI design loop, and the alloy is what lets it run a hotter preburner or turbine, or a higher chamber pressure, than its heritage alloys allow. A drop-in part at the old operating point does not count; that is materials-ai-alloy-flight.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No engine has been designed around an AI-designed alloy (general). Oxygen-rich staged-combustion engines already depend on purpose-built alloys, such as SpaceX's in-house SX500 superalloy for Raptor and NASA's GRCop family for chambers (general). NASA's GRX-810 targets service above about 1,100 C and has not flown in an engine.
add_nodes.why: The first AI-alloy flight (2030 in S2 and S3) is a substitution at the old operating point. The payoff comes when an engine version is designed around the new alloy's margin. A major engine version takes about 3 years, about 2-2.5 years by 2035 in S2-S3 (gate table 0.7-0.8x), and the alloy also needs production powder lots and in-house allowables from several heats. Chain (S2): alloy flight 2030 + creep and oxidation life models (2029) back the design margin -> version designed around the alloy 2031 -> hot-fire campaign and first flight 2033. S3: 2032. S1: alloy flight 2033 -> after 2035. Oxygen-rich preburners and turbines are limited by their alloys' temperature (general), so the gain is performance or life. S2 is Low by 2035 because engine makers may not disclose that an in-house alloy came from an AI loop; S3 is Medium. Robots do not shorten multi-heat alloy lots or 1,000-10,000 h tests, and alloy suppliers robotize only after 2031, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Engine makers already design proprietary alloys without AI (SX500), so attribution is hard to see. A hotter preburner buys a few percent of specific impulse or thrust-to-weight, and reuse economics turn on reliability more than on peak performance.
add_nodes.signpost: An engine maker states that a new engine version's preburner temperature, turbine inlet temperature or chamber pressure rose because of an AI-designed alloy, with hot-fire data.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the performance step after the first AI-alloy flight, 2032-33 in S2-S3. S4 equals S3 because multi-heat alloy lots and long property tests bind, and alloy suppliers robotize only after 2031.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the alloy chain past materials-ai-alloy-flight.

add_nodes.title: A new large engine flies four years after program start
add_nodes.description: A clean-sheet liquid rocket engine of at least 1 MN (about 225,000 lbf) thrust flies on an orbital-class launch within four years of its program start, as disclosed by the developer. Derivatives of an existing engine family do not count.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Clean-sheet engines take 6-13 years (model gate table). BE-4 went from program start in 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (general). Raptor work began about 2012; it first flew on a hop in 2019 and on an orbital-class flight in 2023 (general). LEAP 71's Noyron took two 20 kN engines from specification to first flame in under three weeks (Dec 2025), but large engines are paced by hot-fire failure discovery. SpaceX's McGregor site has 15 engine test stands (S-1/A).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability and physical-gate premise; no catalog family)
add_nodes.why: Design labor is already near zero for small engines. Large engines are paced by turbopump and combustion failures that appear only in hot fire, each costing a redesign and a re-test. The gate table puts a new engine at 0.7-0.8x of its 6-13 years in S3 by 2031 and about 10% faster by 2035, so four years needs a best-case program that starts with S3 tools about 2029 (2033, Low). S2 compresses less (about 0.7-0.85x by 2035), so only a program started about 2031 that avoids a major test-stand loss fits (2035, Low). This is the one node in the branch where robots earn S4 credit. A robot-first firm builds several development engines in parallel and turns stands around 24/7, and the gate table gives a leading firm 0.45-0.51x by 2035. All four conditions hold: development is partly labor- and throughput-bound (35% labor), robots are useful at leading firms from 2030-31, no hard prerequisite lands later, and parallel robot-built development engines are not the specialized automation counted in S3. The credit is one band, Low to Medium. The year stays 2033 because a program must start by about 2029-30 to fly by then. Stability prediction and turbopump tools cut redesign loops but are not required.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Fast firms already iterate on cheap printed hardware, so the four-year mark may be set by funding and test-stand losses (BE-4 stand explosions in 2015 and 2023, general), whatever the tools or robots. Few clean-sheet engines of this size start in any five-year period, so the chance rests on two or three programs.
add_nodes.signpost: A developer announces a clean-sheet 1 MN-class engine program in 2028-31 and reports full-duration hot fire within two years; disclosed robot counts at engine factories and test stands.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. This is where S4 differs in this branch: robot-built parallel development engines and 24/7 stand turnaround lift S4 from Low to Medium by 2035. The year stays 2033 because programs must start before robots are useful.

add_nodes.title: Engines fly 50 missions without overhaul
add_nodes.description: Main engines on a heavy reusable launcher fly 50 or more missions each without removal for overhaul, with inspection intervals and retirement limits set by calibrated life models and fleet data, as disclosed by the operator.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 boosters have flown about 30 times each (general), with Merlin engines refurbished between campaigns. Raptor 3 first flew in May 2026 and had logged more than 40,000 s of runtime by Apr 2026 (newspaceeconomy). Mach33's base case has Starship flights per stack rising from 3.3 (2027) to 18 (2030).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise on an exogenous launch clock)
add_nodes.why: Each life data point costs a flight, so this node rides the launch exponential. At Mach33's 18 flights per stack in 2030 and more after, a fleet-leader engine passes 50 flights 2-3 years after the operator stops pulling engines for routine overhaul. Model-based reuse life (prop-reuse-extended, 2029 in S2 and S3) lets the operator stretch intervals step by step without a teardown at each step. Chain (S2): model-based intervals 2029 -> 100+ heavy flights a year 2030 -> fleet leaders at 20-30 flights a year -> 50 flights without overhaul 2033. S3: 2032, with cadence a year earlier. S1: 2034, on the same launch clock with slower, more conservative life models. It stays Medium because one engine-caused failure resets the practice and the operator must disclose it. Robotic inspection and refurbishment shorten turnaround, worth about half a year within 2032 at a robot-first operator, but pads and flights bind more than labor, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Operators may stretch life empirically just as fast, and engine design (Raptor 3 was built for long life) matters more than models. The gains are internal and may not be disclosed.
add_nodes.signpost: An operator discloses engine flight counts above 50 without removal, or NASA or a defense customer accepts a mission on engines past a model-set life limit.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the operating maturity of model-based reuse, reached 2032-34 as heavy cadence passes hundreds of flights a year. S4 gains about half a year inside 2032 from robotic refurbishment; flights bind, so its year and band equal S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the reuse chain past prop-reuse-extended.

add_nodes.title: Propellant sold in orbit to outside customers
add_nodes.description: A depot operator delivers cryogenic propellant in orbit to at least one customer outside its own company, priced per delivered tonne, with the delivered mass measured to an agreed accuracy (custody transfer).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No propellant has been sold in orbit (general). Eta Space targets a commercial LOX depot, Cryo-Dock, by 2030 (satnews, May 2026), informed by the LOXSAT demonstration. SpaceX's refueling is internal to its own lunar-lander contract.
add_nodes.why: Selling propellant needs routine transfers (prop-cislunar-propellant-economy: 2030 in S2), a customer and a measured delivered mass. Gauging with proven error bounds (prop-mass-gauging) and validated boil-off models make custody transfer contractible: at 1% gauging error, a 100 t delivery carries a 1 t dispute (illustrative). Customers would be third-party landers, NASA vehicles outside the lunar-lander contract and other operators' Mars missions; Cryo-Dock aims at LOX. Chain (S2): routine transfers 2030 -> an interface standard and a first contract 2031-32 -> first metered sale 2033. S3: 2032. S1: 2034. Low in S2 because a vertically integrated SpaceX may never sell propellant, and third-party depots need their own launches and customers. Medium in S3, where cadence and demand arrive a year earlier. Launches and customers bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: The stake of better models is small (about 0-1 tanker of margin per campaign), and the market may not exist: SpaceX fuels its own ships, and others may not build compatible vehicles before 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: A signed contract for propellant delivered in orbit to an outside customer, or Cryo-Dock receiving and dispensing propellant.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the commercial end of the refueling chain, 2032-34. Customers and launches bind, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; gives prop-mass-gauging a downstream use (custody transfer).

add_nodes.title: Tankers fuel five Mars ships for one window
add_nodes.description: In the months before one Mars launch window, tankers fill five or more Mars-bound Starships in Earth orbit, and the ships depart in that window. The ships may carry cargo or crew.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: The late-2026 Mars window is being skipped (model). Later windows open about Dec 2028-Jan 2029, early 2031, Apr 2033 and mid 2035 (model). NASA's OIG (Mar 2026) says a lunar-lander refueling needs more than 10 tankers; a Mars ship needs a comparable full refill.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not mainly an AI-math implication: windows, launch cadence and ship readiness set the date. Five ships need roughly 40-75 tanker flights in a few months (illustrative, at 100-150 t per tanker), so the campaign needs 100+ heavy flights a year and routine transfers. Fuelled ships may wait weeks in orbit for departure, so boil-off margin sets the tanker count and the departure order; validated boil-off and transfer models (prop-cfm-models) trim that margin by a few tanker flights per campaign at most. Chain (S3): routine transfers 2029 -> first Mars flights in the Dec 2028-Jan 2029 window -> five-ship campaign for the early-2031 window (Low). S2: routine transfers 2030 -> Apr 2033 window. S1: transfers 2032 -> mid-2035 window. Medium by 2035 in S2-S4: two windows remain, but SpaceX's Mars plans have slipped before, and a missed window costs 26 months. Orbital mechanics fix the window, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics is off the critical path, which runs through cadence, ship reliability and funding. SpaceX may fly fewer, larger campaigns or skip windows.
add_nodes.signpost: SpaceX manifests five or more ships for the Apr 2033 window; a surge of tanker flights in the quarter before a window.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: the Mars-window end of the refueling chain (Apr 2033 and mid-2035 windows). Orbital mechanics fix the dates, so S4 equals S3.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-engines-materials (2026-10-07): new node for the 2035 horizon; extends the refueling chain past prop-cislunar-propellant-economy.

patch.thesis: Certified flow, combustion and materials models give engines model-based reuse life from about 2029 (base case), and an AI-designed alloy likely flies by 2035. In 2032-35 come alloy-enabled engines, 50-flight engine life and Mars-window fueling. Hot fire, creep tests and flights set the pace. Robots (S4) mainly shorten new-engine programs.
patch.reader_hook: A 10,000-hour creep test takes about 14 months, with or without robots. Proving 0.99 engine reliability at 90% confidence takes about 230 zero-failure starts, and one Starship flight logs about 65-70. So by the 2030s engine starts pile up fast, and the pace is set by finding and fixing failure modes and by the long tests behind each new alloy.
